pedagogy.summary: Multiplying a fraction by a fraction (and by a whole number), understood as 'a fraction OF a fraction': (a/b) × (c/d) takes a/b of c/d, computed as (a×c)/(b×d) and written in simplest form. The area model makes it visible — shade c/d of a square one way, then a/b of that the other way, and the overlap is the product. The key realisations are that you multiply straight across (no common denominator, unlike addition) and that the product of two proper fractions is SMALLER than either factor, because you are taking part of a part.
bestPractices: Read the product as 'of': 2/3 × 4/5 is two-thirds OF four-fifths, and model it as a fraction of a fraction.
Use the area/'redefine the unit' model (IES Fig 7): shade one fraction vertically, the other horizontally, the crosshatch is the product over the b×d grid.
Establish that you multiply numerators and denominators directly — explicitly contrast with addition, which needs a common denominator, to block the imported rule.
Use estimation/benchmarks so a product smaller than both factors is expected (1/2 of 1/2 is 1/4), refuting 'multiplication makes bigger'.
Simplify products and, where possible, simplify before multiplying; convert improper products to mixed numbers.
Fold in the whole-number case (2/3 × 4 = 8/3) as c/d with d = 1.
keyRepresentations: Area model: unit square partitioned b×d, one fraction shaded each way, product = overlapping tiles
'Fraction of a fraction' bar: take c/d of the whole, then a/b of that piece
Number line for the fraction × whole case
Equation (a×c)/(b×d) aligned with the shaded grid count
commonMisconceptions: Leaves the denominator unchanged (2/3 × 1/3 = 2/3), over-generalising the common-denominator rule from addition to multiplication (IES).
Seeks a common denominator before multiplying, importing the addition procedure unnecessarily.
Believes the product must be bigger than the factors, so distrusts a smaller answer.
Computes the product but leaves it unsimplified (6/12 rather than 1/2).

learn.summary: Multiplying a fraction by a fraction, understood as 'a fraction OF a fraction': (a/b) × (c/d) takes a/b of c/d, computed as (a×c)/(b×d) and written in simplest form. An area model makes it visible — shade c/d of a unit square one way, a/b of that the other way, and the overlap is the product. The key realisations: you multiply straight across (no common denominator, unlike addition), and the product of two nonzero proper fractions is SMALLER than either factor, because you are taking part of a part. The whole-number case (2/3 × 4 = 8/3) folds in as c/d with d = 1: 2/3 of 4 means splitting 4 into 3 equal parts and taking 2 of them, which equals four copies of 2/3. For a whole number greater than 1, the product is larger than the fraction factor (for 1 it is equal, for 0 it is 0).

activities.title: Two-way area shader: a fraction of a fraction
feedback: If the overlap puzzles the learner, point to the two striped strips: the crosshatch is the region that is BOTH two-thirds and four-fifths-shaded — a smaller block inside both.
When a product like 6/12 appears, prompt: 'Can 6/12 be written with smaller numbers?' and check on the grid that 6/12 and 1/2 cover the same region.

A running 'is the answer bigger or smaller than each factor?' readout (where available) shows that for two PROPER fractions, taking part of a part gives a product smaller than either; note that the whole-number case (2/3 × 4 = 8/3) instead grows beyond the fraction factor 2/3, because it is repeated copies rather than a part of a part.
activities.rationale: A fraction of a fraction is exactly the two-way-shaded area model; partitioning both ways and highlighting the overlap makes 'product = crosshatched tiles' and 'smaller than each proper factor' concrete and manipulable. Letting the learner build and vary the shading, rather than view a finished picture, is where the understanding is constructed.
sourceClaims: Students often leave the denominator unchanged in fraction multiplication (e.g. 2/3 × 1/3 = 2/3) by over-generalising the addition procedure; teach the conceptual basis with the area model ('redefine the unit', Fig 7: 1/4 of 2/3) and unit fractions, showing 1/2 × 1/2 = half of a half = 1/4, so the product is smaller than either factor.

Multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction, interpret (a/b) × q as a parts of a partition of q into b parts, find area of a rectangle with fractional sides by tiling, and write products in simplest form.
learnerActions: Shade 4/5 of a unit square with vertical stripes.
Shade 2/3 of the square with horizontal stripes, over the same region.
Watch the square rule itself into a 3×5 grid of fifteenths; count the crosshatched overlap (8 tiles) and read the product as 8/15.
Repeat for 3/4 × 2/3: see the overlap as 6 tiles out of 12, then use a simplify step to collapse 6/12 to 1/2 on the same picture.
Say each product in words using 'of': '2/3 × 4/5 is two-thirds OF four-fifths.'

Fold in a whole-number case: model 2/3 × 4 (as 2/3 × 4/1) using four unit squares, splitting each into thirds and shading 2/3 of each (equivalently, splitting the 4 wholes into 3 equal parts and taking 2), and read off 8 thirds = 8/3 = 2 2/3; optionally show the same on a number line, jumping 2/3 four times to land on 8/3.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplying two proper fractions means taking a part of a part; the crosshatched overlap sits plainly INSIDE both striped regions, so the product is smaller than either proper factor, and the b×d grid gives the denominator automatically (no common denominator needed). The whole-number case is different: 2/3 × 4 is four copies of 2/3, so 8/3 is larger than 2/3.

activities.title: Contrast multiplication with the addition rule
feedback: If the learner keeps a denominator unchanged (2/3 × 1/3 → 2/3), model on the grid that 2/3 of 1/3 is a small block — 2/9 of the whole (2 tiles of 9), not 2/3.

If the learner hunts a common denominator first, ask which operation this is and whether equal-sized parts are needed to combine (that is addition); show the grid gives fifteenths automatically from 3×5 for 2/3 × 4/5.
activities.rationale: The leave-the-denominator and seek-a-common-denominator errors come from importing the addition schema. Explicitly contrasting the two operations on the same visual blocks the imported rule rather than just correcting the symbol manipulation.
sourceClaims: Students often leave the denominator unchanged in fraction multiplication (e.g. 2/3 × 1/3 = 2/3) by over-generalising the addition procedure; teach the conceptual basis with the area model ('redefine the unit', Fig 7: 1/4 of 2/3) and unit fractions, showing 1/2 × 1/2 = half of a half = 1/4, so the product is smaller than either factor.
learnerActions: Work out 2/3 × 1/3 on the area grid: shade 1/3 one way, take 2/3 of it the other way, and count the overlap — 2 tiles out of 9, i.e. 2/9.
State explicitly: the answer is NOT 2/3; two-thirds OF one-third is smaller than one-third.

Compare side by side with an addition problem that needs re-partitioning (e.g. 2/3 + 4/5): notice addition needs same-sized parts (a common denominator) before you can combine, while multiplication splits the unit BOTH ways and the b×d grid supplies the denominator.
Explain in words why you do not need a common denominator to multiply.
activities.intendedInsight: Multiplication and addition of fractions run different procedures: addition needs a common denominator to combine like-sized parts; multiplication multiplies across because you are partitioning the unit in two directions.

activities.title: Compute and simplify (practice and self-check)
feedback: For a product that keeps an original denominator (e.g. 8/5 or 8/3 written for 2/3 × 4/5), point back to the grid: the tiles are fifteenths because the square was split 3×5, so the answer is 8/15.
For a correct but unsimplified answer (6/12), do not reteach the multiplication — it is right; only prompt for simplest form.
Use the benchmark 1/2 of 1/2 = 1/4 to confirm that a smaller-than-both answer is expected for two proper fractions, not an error.
activities.rationale: A scorable practice set can deliberately bait the leave-denominator and need-common-denominator errors and can isolate whether the simplifying step is secure. Recognition/fill-in items consolidate and diagnose; they check fluency rather than building the initial 'part of a part' concept, so they follow the construction activities.
sourceClaims: Multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction, interpret (a/b) × q as a parts of a partition of q into b parts, find area of a rectangle with fractional sides by tiling, and write products in simplest form.
learnerActions: Complete fill-in-the-blank items of the form '2/3 × 4/5 = __/__ = __ (simplest form)'.
Answer a multiple-choice item for 2/3 × 1/3 where '2/3' (denominator left unchanged) is offered as a tempting wrong answer, and choose/justify the correct 2/9.
Finish a problem that yields 6/12 and reduce it to 1/2 as a required step.
Estimate before computing: predict whether each product is bigger or smaller than its factors.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluency: multiply numerators and denominators directly, always put the result in simplest form, and expect the product of two proper fractions to be smaller than each factor.

constraints: Read every product as 'of' first (2/3 × 4/5 = two-thirds OF four-fifths) and model it before computing symbolically.
Explicitly contrast with addition: multiplication multiplies straight across and needs no common denominator; raise this whenever a learner tries to find one.
Always put products in simplest form, and where possible simplify before multiplying; convert improper products to mixed numbers (8/3 = 2 2/3).
The practice items check fluency and bait known errors; they do not by themselves build the 'part of a part' meaning, so pair them with the area-model construction rather than substitute for it.

A static finished picture (e.g. tapping to reveal 8/15 on a pre-shaded square) can serve as a reference anchor, but it does not let the learner build the shading or vary the factors, which is where the understanding forms — use it as a supplement, not the main activity.
The area model is planar; a flat grid is the natural representation here and a 3D rendering is not needed for this objective.

The claim 'product is smaller than either factor' is scoped to two nonzero proper fractions; when a proper fraction multiplies a whole number greater than 1, the product (e.g. 2/3 × 4 = 8/3) is smaller than the whole number but larger than the proper fraction factor.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/15 (correct); 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 = 1/2 (correct); 2/3 × 1/3 = 2/9 (correct); 2/3 × 4 = 8/3 = 2 2/3 (correct). The original row's next-move text said '2/3 of 1/3 is a small block, one-ninth of the whole': that is imprecise — 2/3 OF 1/3 = 2/9 (2 tiles of 9), while 1/9 would be 1/3 of 1/3. Activities use the corrected value 2/9 for 2/3 × 1/3; the mistaken 1/9 is recorded here only, never offered as a learner option.

The 'smaller than either factor' narrative is scoped to proper fractions throughout; activity[0] mixes proper×proper with the whole-number case, so the readout feedback now explicitly flags that 2/3 × 4 = 8/3 grows beyond 2/3 because it is repeated copies.

The original keyRepresentations list includes a number line for the fraction × whole-number case; it is retained as an optional scaffold in the whole-number action (2/3 jumped four times to 8/3) so the distinct representation is not lost.
CCSS/DfE source is marked verified:false in the row; treat it as a standards-alignment reference rather than evidence of efficacy.
Source claims cite the teaching principle (area model, multiply across, simplest form); they do not establish that the specific interactive shader described has been empirically tested.

probeDeeper: Say 2/3 × 4/5 in words using 'of' — what are you taking a part of? Show it on an area picture.
A friend says 2/3 × 1/3 = 2/3. But two-thirds OF one-third — is that bigger or smaller than 1/3? Can it be 2/3?
Do you need a common denominator to multiply? How is that different from adding?
Is 6/12 finished? Write it as simply as you can — how do you know it's the same amount?
assess.correctAnswer: 2/3 × 4/5 = 8/15. 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 = 1/2. Multiply numerators and denominators directly (no common denominator), then simplify.

errorPatterns.pattern: Leaves the denominator unchanged: '2/3 × 1/3 = 2/3' or keeps a shared denominator in the answer — imports the addition (common-denominator) rule into multiplication.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model on the area grid: 2/3 of 1/3 is a small block, one-ninth of the whole — not 2/3. Contrast explicitly: addition needs a common denominator, multiplication does not; here you split the unit BOTH ways (b×d).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Product keeps one of the original denominators unchanged; for 2/3 × 4/5 may write 8/5 or 8/3.

errorPatterns.pattern: Finds a common denominator before multiplying, converting 2/3 and 4/5 to fifteenths and then mis-combining — applies the addition setup to a multiplication.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask what operation this is and whether it needs equal-sized parts to combine (no — that's addition). Multiply across; show the grid gives fifteenths automatically from 3×5.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Rewrites both fractions over a common denominator as a first step for a multiplication; often then adds or muddles.

errorPatterns.pattern: Multiplies correctly but leaves the answer unsimplified: writes 6/12 and stops.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach multiplying — it's correct. Prompt: 'can 6/12 be written with smaller numbers?' Check on the grid that 6/12 and 1/2 are the same region.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Correct unsimplified product (6/12); the operation is right, only simplest form is missing.

responseLevels.gap: Leaves the denominator unchanged or seeks a common denominator (importing the addition rule); products don't come from multiplying across.
responseLevels.full: Computes (a/b) × (c/d) = ac/bd, simplifies (6/12 → 1/2), justifies with an area or 'fraction of a fraction' model, recognises the product of proper fractions is smaller than each; transfers to a new pair including a whole number.
responseLevels.partial: Multiplies across correctly for the straightforward case but forgets to simplify, or can't justify with an area model / explain why the product is smaller — procedure without meaning.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Work these out, showing how (a picture is fine): 2/3 × 4/5, and 3/4 × 2/3. Give each answer in its simplest form.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Multiplying straight across contrasts with the addition habit: a child who leaves the denominator unchanged (2/3 × 1/3 → 2/3) or hunts a common denominator reveals they're running the addition procedure. 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 is chosen to require simplifying, isolating whether that final step is secure. Both products are smaller than their factors, probing whether the child accepts 'a fraction of a fraction is smaller'. Watching the method shows which operation's schema is running.
